habitat.description: Giant pandas inhabit cool, wet bamboo forests in the mountainous regions of central China, typically between 1,500 and 3,000 meters elevation. They depend almost entirely on bamboo, consuming 12-38 kilograms daily across up to 60 different bamboo species. The fragmented mountain forests they occupy represent less than 1% of their historical range.

threats.name: Habitat Fragmentation
threats.description: Roads, railways, and development split panda habitat into isolated patches, preventing movement between populations.

threats.name: Bamboo Die-offs
threats.description: Bamboo species periodically flower and die en masse. In fragmented habitats, pandas cannot move to alternative bamboo sources.

threats.name: Small Population Size
threats.description: Many subpopulations are too small to be genetically viable long-term, increasing vulnerability to disease and inbreeding.

threats.name: Climate Change
threats.description: Shifting climate zones may reduce suitable bamboo habitat at higher elevations, further constraining available range.

conservationStatus.population: Approximately 1,864 individuals in the wild (2014 census), with population increasing
keyPrograms: Captive breeding and reintroduction at Chengdu and Bifengxia

culturalSignificance.overview: The giant panda is perhaps the most recognizable conservation symbol on Earth, serving as the logo of the World Wildlife Fund since 1961. In Chinese culture, the panda represents peace and friendship. Its dramatic recovery from fewer than 1,000 individuals to a growing population demonstrates that sustained conservation investment can reverse decline.
